newsitem.title: UK: Oasis threatens Internet sites over copyright.
newsitem.headline: Oasis threatens Internet sites over copyright.

text.p: Britain's top-selling rock band Oasis has issued a legal warning over the use of copyright material on hundreds of unofficial Internet sites dedicated to the group.
The band's management said on Thursday it hoped that website operators would heed the warning and not force the group to go to law.

"I don't think it will come to that (legal action)," said band spokesman Johnny Hopkins. "Our aim is not to close down sites. We want to make people aware of the rules and our hope is that people will comply."
Unofficial Oasis websites have been using extensive sound and video material from the band without permission.
"It is this sort of behaviour that we have to discourage," the band's management company Ignition said in a statement.
"After all taking something without asking permission can be seen as theft and in this case the people concerned could be seen to be stealing from the band they claim to support."
Some Oasis fans who run Internet page were upset by an e-mail message last week advising they had 30 days to remove unauthorised material from their pages or face legal action.

Oasis Webmasters for Internet Freedom, which groups together Oasis Internet operators, then publicly posted the e-mail, which said: "This is a very serious warning. Failure to comply with the law will ultimately result in legal action."
Ignition said the band had always encouraged fan pages that "make a fun and interesting contribution to Oasis on the net".
But it added: "There are a number of sites out there who to be frank we feel have taken advantage of this situation.
"In particular a number of pages have been copying freely from the official homepage without bothering to ask permission or give the homepage a credit."
While some Oasis Internet sites are the work of fans, others are devoted to trading bootleg Oasis recordings -- often recordings of concerts and television appearances by the group.

Oasis, whose first two albums have sold 20 million copies, have led a "Britpop" revival, but feuding between band member brothers Noel and Liam Gallagher has generated as many headlines as the music. Oasis's record company Creation is 49 percent owned by Sony Music.
